lessons.title: Your team's identity
lessons.objective: You can say what {{team}} is known for.

statement.speaker: Friend
statement.text: {{team}} has a totally different vibe than the rest of the league.

payload.question: What is your friend saying?

options.text: {{team}} plays or coaches the same way as other teams.
{{team}} has a recognizable style, culture or reputation that sets them apart.
{{team}} is always going to lose.
{{team}} only plays on Sundays.

payload.translation: Team identity is what makes {{team}} recognizable: their style of play, how their coaches think, who their stars are, what they build around. It is what fans see and care about.

followUps.line: What makes {{team}} different from their division rivals?
followUps.why: Identity means being distinct even from neighbors you know well.

followUps.line: Has {{team}}'s identity changed over the last five years?
followUps.why: Identities evolve with new coaches and stars.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, think about what you hear about {{team}} first: aggressive, ball-control, risk-taking, steady. That is identity.

payload.prompt: What does team identity include?

options.text: How the team plays offense and defense, the coach's system, the star players, and what fans talk about.
Only the color of their uniform.
How many wins they had last year.

explanation.correct: Team identity is the whole package: the scheme, the culture, the key players. It is what makes {{team}} sound like {{team}} when fans talk about them.
explanation.incorrect: Team identity goes way deeper than colors or one-year records. It is the core personality of the team.

payload.prompt: You can learn {{team}}'s identity by watching a few games and talking to their fans. True or false?

scene.alt: Fans and analysts talking about what makes a team unique.

explanation.correct: True. Team identity shows up in play-calling, player types, and fan culture. A few games and some listening are enough.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, identity is visible. Watch how they line up, how they adjust, who they draft and sign. It becomes clear fast.

payload.prompt: Match the identity trait to what it means.

pairs.definition: Known for throwing often, spreading defenses out, and valuing receivers and pass-catchers.
Built on running the ball, controlling the clock, and valuing powerful blockers and patient backs.
Known for smothering opposing offenses, forcing turnovers, and building stars on that side of the ball.

explanation.summary: Every team leans toward one identity: how they attack and what they value in players.
explanation.sayThisLine: Teams are pass-heavy, run-heavy or defense-focused. {{team}} is {{team}}'s thing.

payload.prompt: What is the strongest part of a team's identity?

facts.label: Star players
facts.value: Hall of famers and future greats

options.label: The coach's system
options.consequence: The system lasts. Players come and go, but the scheme and culture endure.

options.label: The star players
options.consequence: Stars are important, but they embody the system, not define it alone.

payload.expertNote: Team identity is built on the system first. Players execute it; coaches design it.

lessons.title: How {{team}} plays
lessons.objective: You can describe {{team}}'s offense and defense in one line each.

payload.prompt: Match {{team}}'s offensive choices to their style.

pairs.definition: Shotgun and empty mean pass. Under center with a back means run.
Many receivers = passing team. Heavy backs = run team.
Lots of movement before the snap shows complexity or pass-heavy.

explanation.summary: {{team}}'s offense shows its identity in lineup, formation and pace.
explanation.sayThisLine: Watch how {{team}} lines up and you know what they will do.

payload.prompt: How can you read {{team}}'s offensive style before the snap?

options.text: Look at the formation, count receivers, and see if the quarterback is in shotgun or under center.
Wait for the play to start and see what happens.
Count how many times the crowd cheers.

explanation.correct: {{team}}'s pre-snap look tells you if they are passing or running. Shotgun and empty backfield mean pass. Under center and a back next to the QB mean run.
explanation.incorrect: You do not have to wait. {{team}}'s style is visible pre-snap in how they line up.

payload.prompt: Defenses are either aggressive blitzers or patient coverage teams. True or false?

scene.alt: A blitzing defense attacking and a patient coverage defense reading the play.

explanation.correct: True. Defenses have personalities too. {{team}}'s defense is either aggressive and risky or disciplined and safe.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, every defense has an identity. {{team}}'s defensive coordinator builds one and sticks to it.

payload.prompt: Match the defensive identity to its approach.

pairs.definition: Play zone, keep everything in front, limit big plays, trust the pass rush to generate pressure.
Blitz often, play man coverage, take risks to create turnovers and disrupt plays early.
Mix blitz and coverage, adjust on the fly, stay unpredictable.

explanation.summary: {{team}}'s defense has a personality. Once you know it, you can predict how they respond.
explanation.sayThisLine: {{team}}'s defense is mostly (patient/aggressive/mixed). That is their style.

payload.prompt: {{team}} drafted three RBs early but still throws most. Does identity change?

facts.label: Draft
facts.value: Three running backs in early rounds

options.label: Yes, identity is shifting
options.consequence: Identities do change, especially with new personnel. But watch the actual play-calling.
considerations: One draft class is not a shift yet.
New personnel might just be depth.

options.label: No, same coach means same identity
options.consequence: True. Identity is the coach's system first. {{team}} is still pass-heavy until the play-calling proves otherwise.
considerations: Drafting backs might just add depth.
Watch how they use them in game.

payload.expertNote: Team identity is durable. One draft class does not shift years of identity. Identity shifts when the coach changes or the team stops doing what they always do.

lessons.title: The players to know
lessons.objective: You can name three players and their roles.

payload.prompt: Match key positions to why they matter.

pairs.definition: The face of the team. {{player}} shapes how {{team}} plays.
The best receiver or tight end. Second name in pass-heavy teams.
The player who embodies {{team}}'s run or defense identity.

explanation.summary: Every team has key stars. Know them and you know {{team}}'s identity.
explanation.sayThisLine: {{team}} is built around {{player}}, (second star), and (third star). That is {{team}}.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: If {{player}} is healthy, {{team}} can compete. He is the whole offense.

payload.question: What is the fan saying?

options.text: {{player}} is the only good player on {{team}}.
{{player}} is the most important player to {{team}}'s success and health.
{{team}} has no other good players.
The quarterback never gets injured.

payload.translation: Star players carry their teams. {{player}}'s health and performance change everything about what {{team}} can do.

followUps.line: What happens to {{team}} if {{player}} gets injured?
followUps.why: The backup and depth matter. Some teams have good backups, others fall apart.

followUps.line: Is {{player}} the most important player on {{team}}?
followUps.why: Knowing the pecking order of stars tells you how {{team}} is built.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, think: which player does every fan talk about first? That is the star.

payload.prompt: How many {{team}} stars should you know to join a conversation?

options.text: At least three: the quarterback or top offensive skill player, and two more who shape {{team}}'s identity.
You need to know the entire 53-man roster.
Just the team name is enough.

explanation.correct: {{team}} fans will talk about their stars. Know the top three and you can follow and ask smart follow-ups.
explanation.incorrect: You do not need the whole roster. Just the names that come up in conversation first.

payload.prompt: If {{player}} gets injured, {{team}}'s identity changes.

explanation.correct: True. Star injuries reshape {{team}}. The backup fills in but changes the team.
explanation.incorrect: {{player}} is central to {{team}}. An injury forces adjustments.

payload.prompt: The backup quarterback is almost as important to {{team}}'s identity as the starter. True or false?

scene.alt: A starter and a backup quarterback on the sideline.

explanation.correct: False. The starter defines {{team}}. The backup is important if injury happens, but does not shape {{team}}'s identity.
explanation.incorrect: The starter is what {{team}} is about. The backup is depth for emergencies.

lessons.title: Division rivals
lessons.objective: You can name the rivals and why they matter.

payload.prompt: Why do division rivals matter more than any other opponent?

options.text: You play them twice a year, they block your playoff path, and there is years of history and fan culture between you.
They are in a different city.
Division games always go to overtime.

explanation.correct: Division rivals are your neighbors and your obstacles. Twice a year for years builds real beef.
explanation.incorrect: Division games matter because they are frequent, they shape the playoffs, and fans care deeply.

statement.speaker: Analyst
statement.text: {{team}} and (rival name) split every year. You never count on sweeping them.

payload.question: What is the analyst saying?

options.text: {{team}} should never play this rival.
Rivalry games are unpredictable. Even if {{team}} is better, the rival can steal one.
{{team}} wins every game.
Rivalry games are decided before they are played.

payload.translation: Rivalry games do not follow the records. The beef, the history, the division stakes make them unpredictable. {{team}} can lose even when they should win.

followUps.line: Why would a worse team beat a better team in a rivalry game?
followUps.why: Because rivalries add intensity and familiarity that flips outcomes.

followUps.line: What makes (rival name) {{team}}'s most important rival?
followUps.why: Some divisions have one big rivalry, others are balanced. It depends on who is competitive.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, just remember: division games are personal and unpredictable.

payload.prompt: Put the playoff stakes in order from closest to most distant.

items.text: Winning your division guarantees a playoff spot.
items.why: Division winners are seeds 1-4 and make the playoffs automatically.

items.text: Winning your conference but not your division makes you a wild card.
items.why: You are in the conference playoff race but not guaranteed a seed.

items.text: Losing to division rivals costs you the division and pushes you to a wild card race.
items.why: Division losses directly impact your standing and can cost you the division.

explanation.correct: Division games are the most impactful. They count twice and directly determine your playoff chances.
explanation.incorrect: Playoff structure matters: division winner first, then wildcards. Every division game is a must-win.

payload.prompt: All four division rivals are equally competitive with {{team}}. True or false?

scene.alt: Three rival teams with different strengths competing for the division.

explanation.correct: False. One rival is often the big one; others might be stronger or weaker. {{team}} fans care most about the main rival.
explanation.incorrect: Divisions are not balanced. {{team}} has one or two big rivals they care about most.

payload.prompt: {{team}} and a rival are tied. One game decides the division.

facts.label: Playoff path
facts.value: Division winner gets a seed; loser fights for wild card

facts.label: History
facts.value: Split the first two matchups this year

options.label: This is the biggest game of the season
options.consequence: Correct. Division down to one game is as important as it gets. {{team}} fans are screaming.

options.label: Even if {{team}} loses, they will get a wild card.
options.consequence: No. Wild card is not guaranteed. A loss here puts {{team}} in a fight for any playoff spot.

payload.expertNote: Division games late in the season are everything. {{team}} fans know this. These are the games that define the season.

lessons.title: Team history
lessons.objective: You can quote one moment in {{team}} history.

statement.speaker: Long-time fan
statement.text: I was there for (historic moment). That game changed everything for {{team}}.

payload.question: What is the fan saying?

options.text: One game does not matter.
Some moments in {{team}} history are so important that fans remember them forever.
Every regular-season game is equally important.
{{team}} has never had a memorable moment.

payload.translation: Every team has moments: a Super Bowl win, a legendary playoff run, a heartbreaking loss, a famous comeback. {{team}}'s fans know theirs and bring them up.

followUps.why: Every team has a defining game or play fans quote forever.
Championships define eras and {{team}}'s whole identity.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, ask a fan. Every team's moment is different and {{team}}'s fans love telling it.

payload.prompt: What kind of {{team}} history moment do fans care about most?

options.text: Playoff runs, championships, famous plays, or breakout seasons that define {{team}}'s era.
Regular-season wins by a touchdown.
Pre-season games.

explanation.correct: {{team}} fans remember the big moments: Super Bowls, Playoff wins, iconic plays. Those are the stories they tell.
explanation.incorrect: Team history is made in big games. Regular season does not carry the same weight in memory.

payload.prompt: Order {{team}}'s eras by approximate time.

items.text: {{team}}'s early years and first decade, when the identity started.
items.why: Every team began somewhere. {{team}}'s foundation shapes how they think now.

items.text: {{team}}'s peak era, if they had one: championships or sustained success.
items.why: If {{team}} had a dynasty (Super Bowls, multiple deep runs), it defines the team and its fans.

items.text: {{team}} now, with current coaching and identity.
items.why: The team today is built on the past but looks forward.

explanation.correct: {{team}}'s timeline shows how they evolved and what eras define them.
explanation.incorrect: Understanding {{team}}'s history means knowing when they were great, when they rebuilt, and where they are now.

payload.prompt: A famous {{team}} moment from 15 years ago is brought up in conversation. Do you have to know all the details?

facts.label: Moment
facts.value: A historic {{team}} playoff game or play

facts.label: Your knowledge
facts.value: You know it happened but not every detail

options.label: Admit you don't know the details and ask them to tell it
options.consequence: Perfect. {{team}} fans love telling their history. Asking invites them in.

options.label: Pretend you remember and make something up
options.consequence: Risky. {{team}} fans know their history cold. Making it up is obvious.

payload.expertNote: {{team}}'s history is theirs. You are learning it. Ask them, and they will tell you what makes it matter.

payload.prompt: Match the historical marker to its meaning.

pairs.definition: {{team}} was starting over: new coach, new scheme, trading stars. Years of lower expectations.
{{team}} was built to win now: stars in their prime, playoff teams, a few Super Bowl runs.
{{team}} was shifting identity: new coach, new quarterback or new direction coming.

explanation.summary: Every team goes through eras. Knowing {{team}}'s era helps you understand where they are heading.
explanation.sayThisLine: {{team}} is in a (rebuild/championship window/transition). That is where they are right now.

lessons.title: How {{team}} fans talk
lessons.objective: You can recognize the chants and complaints.

statement.speaker: Frustrated fan
statement.text: {{team}} always does the same thing and it never works anymore. The coach needs to change it up.

payload.question: What is the fan saying?

options.text: {{team}}'s identity and system are no longer working because the rest of the league has adapted.
{{team}} is the only team with an identity.
The coach never changes anything.
{{team}} has no system.

payload.translation: {{team}} fans know their team's identity so well they notice when it stops working. If opponents figure it out, fans see it first.

followUps.line: How does a team's system get figured out?
followUps.why: Opponents watch film, adjust, and eventually {{team}} has to evolve.

followUps.line: Does {{team}} need a new identity or just new personnel?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, listen. {{team}} fans will explain their own frustrations.

payload.title: Game day with {{team}} fans
payload.setting: At the tailgate or before kickoff.

exchanges.theirMessage: I hate when {{team}} does (typical play call or strategy). It is so predictable.

replies.text: Is that the coach's system or has it just gotten predictable?
replies.theirResponse: Both. The coach has always done it. Other teams know it now.
replies.coachNote: Shows you know about identity and how it can become a weakness.

replies.theirResponse: Right? Like, change it up sometimes.
replies.coachNote: Agreement is fine, but asking why deepens it.

replies.theirResponse: Not when everyone knows it is coming.
replies.coachNote: Do not argue with her expertise. She watches the team.

payload.closingNote: {{team}} fans know their team inside out. Acknowledge what they see.

payload.prompt: Why do {{team}} fans bring up the same complaints over and over?

options.text: Because {{team}}'s problems are usually rooted in their identity and system, which take time to change.
Because they do not understand football.
Because {{team}} fires coaches every week.

explanation.correct: {{team}} fans spot patterns. If the same problem happens over and over, it is the system. They are right.
explanation.incorrect: Fans are not complaining for fun. If {{team}} keeps doing the same thing with bad results, fans see it.

payload.prompt: Match the {{team}} fan phrase to what it means.

pairs.definition: Everyone knows what {{team}} is going to do because they do the same thing every game.
That play or approach is so {{team}}, it is who they are.

pairs.term: Game day starts at the parking lot
pairs.definition: The tailgate before kickoff is a core {{team}} fan ritual.

explanation.summary: {{team}} fans have their own lingo. Understanding it is half the conversation.
explanation.sayThisLine: If {{team}} fans say something is predictable or that is {{team}}'s DNA, they are talking about identity.

payload.prompt: For {{team}} fans, the tailgate is the core ritual.

scene.alt: Fans at a pre-game tailgate party.

explanation.correct: True. Tailgating is how {{team}} fans gather, connect and celebrate.
explanation.incorrect: The tailgate is where {{team}} fans build community.
